title: Embouchure, pressure and King Oliver's deep mouthpiece
summary: Phillips says players used pressure for a big tone; others filed mouthpieces shallow to play high, but Oliver used a cup about an inch deep.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: What kind of embrochure did he have? Did he use a lot of pressure?

Yeah, everybody used pressure back in those days. Louis too. Louis used a lot of pressure. See, that's why Louis had such a big, broad tone. Cats that use this non-pressure, some of them got this little teeny tone, like Maynard Ferguson. See, he don't have no tone on his horn, no big tone. He's got a little small sound, almost like a flute.
He might have one of those small mouthpieces, too, so he can play all those high notes.
I shouldn't say. I don't know anything about trumpet...
Anyway, did King Oliver ever talk about embrochure or anything like that?

See, he'd give the guys the devil, he'd give me the devil too about... See, at that time we used to file our mouthpieces, get a file and file our mouthpieces down so they'd be shallow and you could play high. See, everybody in those days was trying to play high like Louis. Because, see, Louis was playing all those melodies up high, you know what I mean, and everybody was trying to do it. King said, "Louis don't have no mouthpiece filed down." King Oliver's
mouthpiece had a cup in it that deep.
About an inch deep. I used to wonder how he'd make them. He made them just as pretty, them D's and E's.
Well, that mouthpiece is good for low notes, right? An inch deep?
Well, you can make a lower note all the time on a deeper mouthpiece.
But you can still play higher ones.
